stories.text: On the night of 8–9 May 1941 the Luftwaffe bombed Nottingham. Firefighters saved St Mary's Church after an incendiary burned through its roof; three Boots factories, in Poplar Street, Island Street and Station Street, were on fire; University College and the Shakespeare Street chapel were hit. The worst loss was at the Co-op bakery on Meadow Lane, where 49 people died. In all, 159 people were killed that night.

Vera Anderson, a Boots nurse, was on duty when bombs wrecked the Boots Printing Works here on 8 May 1941. She gave first aid to a dying night watchman through burning debris, then treated casualties at the control centre, and was awarded the George Medal.

72531.sum: Trent House is the European headquarters of the finance company Capital One. It is on Station Street to the south of the centre of the English city of Nottingham, opposite Nottingham railway station and adjacent to Loxley House, the administrative headquarters of Nottingham City Council. The building dates from 1951, when it was built as a print works for the pharmaceutical company Boots, whose various premises occupied most of the surrounding area at that time.

stories.text: Nottingham's first station, opened in 1839 by the Midland Counties Railway, stood across Carrington Street; a through station replaced it on this site in 1848. The present building, of red brick and terracotta, was designed by the local architect Albert Edward Lambert and opened on 16 January 1904. Its carriage entrances have Art Nouveau gates of wrought iron. A pair taken down in 1951, made in Leicester in 1904, is now in the Science Museum Group's collection.[^gates]

72578.sum: Nottingham station, briefly known as Nottingham City and for rather longer as Nottingham Midland, is a railway station and tram stop in the city of Nottingham, England. It is the principal railway station of Nottingham. It is also a nodal point on the city's tram system, with a tram stop that was originally called Station Street but is now known as Nottingham Station.

stories.text: In 1500 a tannery was set up in two caves opening onto the cliff face, the only known underground tannery in Britain. Over the years the caves under the old town were also used as pub cellars and as an air raid shelter.

74223.sum: City of Caves is an office building on Middle Pavement.

stories.text: Garners Hill, said to be the oldest site in Nottingham, once held cave dwellings, a Saxon fort and a medieval town hall, until the Victorians cleared it for a railway line. On 14 November 2009 an art centre designed by Caruso St John opened here, its walls embossed with a Nottingham lace pattern.

74224.sum: Nottingham Contemporary (formerly known as the Centre for Contemporary Art Nottingham) is a contemporary art centre in the Lace Market area of Nottingham, England. The gallery opened in 2009. The gallery describes its site as being "the oldest in the city", having been the site of a Saxon fort.

stories.text: On 7 August 1844 William Saville, who had murdered his wife and their three children in Colwick Wood, was hanged in front of the County Hall on High Pavement. A vast crowd had packed the street; the Northern Star put it at no fewer than twenty thousand. As the drop fell the crowd surged, and many were forced down the steps from High Pavement into Garner's Hill and trampled.[^star] Twelve were killed and more than a hundred badly hurt, five of whom died later;[^spectator][^date] one report counted seven dead on the day.[^star] Wikipedia's article on the General Hospital says instead that a stand collapsed.[^gh] The last public hanging in Nottingham was that of Richard Thomas Parker, on 10 August 1864.[^parker]

stories.text: Courts sat on this spot from at least 1375, and prisoners were held here from at least 1449. The hall was rebuilt to a design by James Gandon in 1769–72, and largely rebuilt again after a fire in 1876. In 1864 Richard Thomas Parker was hanged on a scaffold over the front steps, the last public execution here. Courts sat here until 1991, and in 1995 the building opened as a museum, now the National Justice Museum.
The architect James Gandon designed the rebuilt Shire Hall.[^s1][^s2]
National Justice Museum opened in 1995. Subject: buildings: penal.

74251.sum: The National Justice Museum is an independent museum on High Pavement in the Lace Market area of Nottingham, England. The museum is housed in a former Victorian courtroom, prison, and police station and is therefore a historic site where an individual could be arrested, tried, sentenced and executed. The courtrooms date back to the 14th century and the gaol to at least 1449.

stories.text: In 1392 John de Plumptre, a Mayor of Nottingham, founded a hospital here for "thirteen poor women broken down of age and depressed of poverty", with two priests. Huntingdon Plumptre repaired it in 1650, and the present building was begun in 1823. The charity closed in 1991, when it could no longer afford to improve the building, and in 2001 the Royal National Institute for the Blind took it over.

74368.sum: Plumptre Hospital was a charity in Nottingham, England, providing almshouse accommodation for 599 years from 1392 to 1991.

A church stood on this hilltop by 1086, when it was recorded in the Domesday Book. It is one of the three mediaeval parish churches of Nottingham.

74412.sum: The Church of St Mary the Virgin is the oldest parish church in Nottingham, England. The church is Grade I listed by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport as a building of outstanding architectural or historic interest. It is one of only five Grade I listed buildings in the City of Nottingham.

stories.text: The congregation went back to 1690 and became Unitarian in 1802. In 1876 it built this chapel, to designs by Stuart Colman. Worship ended in 1982; the chapel then housed a lace museum, and it is now a Pitcher & Piano.

74438.sum: High Pavement Chapel is a redundant church building in Nottingham, Nottinghamshire, England. It is now the Pitcher & Piano public house and is Grade II listed. It was built as, and for most of its existence operated as, a Unitarian place of worship.

stories.text: Built from 1854 to designs by Thomas Chambers Hine for Thomas Adams, a Quaker lace manufacturer, and opened in 1855 as his lace showroom and warehouse, with a chapel for the workers in the basement. Inspectors thought it a model example of its kind; since 1999 it has been part of Nottingham College.
The lace manufacturer Thomas Adams built this showroom and warehouse; it is named after him.[^s1][^s2]
The Nottingham architect Thomas Chambers Hine designed this lace showroom and warehouse.[^s1][^s2]

74534.sum: The Adams Building, formerly the Adams and Page warehouse on Stoney Street, is the largest building in the Lace Market district of the city of Nottingham in England. Now Grade II*-listed by Historic England, the Adams Building was formerly a lace showroom and warehouse. Since 1999, it has formed part of the city campus of what is now Nottingham College.

stories.text: Watson Fothergill, born Fothergill Watson, took his mother's family name in 1892 and built his own offices here, on George Street, in 1895.[^s1] Its front has a statue of a medieval architect and busts of Augustus Pugin and George Edmund Street; it is listed Grade II.[^s2]

74693.sum: Watson Fothergill’s office is a Grade II listed building in George Street, Nottingham.

76263.sum: Shakespeare Street Wesleyan Reform Chapel is a former Wesleyan Reform church on Shakespeare Street in Nottingham, England, in the United Kingdom. The building was converted in 1953 to a synagogue and is now a university hall. Whilst in use as a synagogue, in 1972 the building was listed as a Grade II building.

Built in 1877–81 for University College Nottingham, with the town's library and a natural history museum, and damaged by bombs in the Second World War. D. H. Lawrence studied here to become a teacher; it is now Nottingham Trent University's Arkwright Building.
Built between 1877 and 1881 for University College Nottingham, where D. H. Lawrence studied during his teacher-training years.[^s1]

76264.sum: The Arkwright Building is a Grade II* listed university building on Shakespeare Street in Nottingham, England. It forms part of the Nottingham Trent University City Campus and is one of the university's principal historic buildings. Built between 1877 and 1881, the building was originally home to University College Nottingham, the city library and a natural history museum.
